items.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000
items.q: I’m in complete accordance with people, with Duke Ellington, Miles Davis, people like that.

ctx.x: My name is Monk Rowe and we’re filming in Manhattan today, and I’m very, very pleased to have Chico Hamilton with me, who has had a long, illustrious and varied career in music. Would you mind telling me what you’re up to in the year 2000?

Sure. I’m just trying to stay alive. No, as a matter of fact we’re up to a whole lot of things. The group, my orchestra — I don’t refer to it as a band, it’s an orchestra, because I think we try to cover all facets of music, not just one direction you know, and not just necessarily under the terminology of even jazz — J-A-Z-Z. I really disapprove of the word myself. I’m in complete accordance with people, with Duke Ellington, Miles Davis, people like that. Why not call it just my music, Chico’s music? Duke…
Right. Does it make a problem, if you’re trying to find a record label to promote your work, they need to put a title to what it is? If you don’t want to call it jazz but they do?

items.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I stayed there -- oh, I must have played about a couple, two or three weeks until Sonny got well.

ctx.x: And what year was this? So you were already married.

No, we weren’t even married. We weren’t married. One of the rare times I took her on a date, took her to the -- we went to the theater, went to see a movie and on the way home, I got to her house, her mother came out on the front porch, she said Forest, there’s a gentleman here waiting for you, to see you, to talk to you. And just then Herb Jeffries got out of the car, came up on the porch. He says Sonny had an accident. They want you to play, come out and play in the band.
Herb Jeffries is waiting out in the car, waiting for you to come back so he can tell you to come sub for Sonny Greer. Herb Jeffries.
